chapters.title: Chapter 2: Yield Measures and What They Really Mean

lessons.title: Yield to Call and Yield to Worst: Pricing Bonds the Issuer Can Redeem Early

children.text: A private banker offers you a 10-year bank bond at an 8% yield to maturity. What the pitch may not mention is that the bank can repay it after just three years, and it will do exactly that if rates fall. Suddenly your "10-year, 8%" bond is a 3-year bond yielding under 7%, and you are reinvesting the proceeds at lower rates. Bank Tier 2 bonds, AT1 bonds and many PSU and NBFC NCDs in India carry such call options. This lesson teaches you to calculate yield to call and yield to worst, so you always know the lowest return you can realistically get.

body.text: A call option belongs to the issuer, and the issuer will use it only when it helps them and hurts you. For any callable bond, assume the worst: the return that matters is the yield to worst.

children.text: What a Call Option Is

markDefs.definition: A bond that the issuer has the right, but not the obligation, to redeem before maturity on specified dates at a specified price.
The price the issuer must pay to redeem the bond early. Often face value, sometimes slightly above it.

children.text: A
callable bond
gives the issuer the right to repay you early, on one or more call dates, at a stated
call price

. Think of it like prepaying a home loan. If your bank's lending rates fall from 9% to 7.5%, you refinance. An issuer paying 8.50% on a bond will do the same when it can raise fresh money at 7%: call the old bond, pay you back, and issue a cheaper one.

body.caption: Where Indian investors meet callable bonds

cells: Long maturity, callable after a minimum of 5 years from issue, with RBI approval
Banks usually call if refinancing is cheaper; secondary buyers may have only a year or two to the call
No maturity; callable after 5 years and on later dates, with RBI approval
No guaranteed repayment at all; coupons can be skipped and the bonds can be written down
Some series carry call (and sometimes put) options on set dates
Check the offer document or information memorandum for every call date and price

children.text: Yield to Call: Same Equation, Different End Date

markDefs.definition: The annualised return if you buy at today's price and the bond is redeemed on a given call date at the call price.

children.text: You already know how to solve for YTM.
Yield to call

uses the identical equation with two changes: the cash flows stop at the call date instead of the maturity date, and the final repayment is the call price instead of face value. Everything else, including the search method and Excel's RATE and YIELD functions, works the same way.

body.caption: n_c = periods until the call date. Shown for an annual-coupon bond, as most Indian bank and corporate bonds pay annually. In Excel on a coupon date: =RATE(periods to call, coupon, −price, call price).

children.text: Worked Example: A Bank Tier 2 Bond at a Premium

An illustrative public sector bank Tier 2 bond: 8.50% annual coupon, 10 years to maturity, callable at par (₹100) in exactly 3 years, and trading on a coupon date at ₹104.50. Market yields have fallen since issue, which is why the price is above par.

Why is the yield to call so much lower? You paid ₹104.50 and will get back ₹100. Held to maturity, that ₹4.50 loss is spread across 10 years. Called in 3 years, the same ₹4.50 loss is squeezed into 3 years, cutting the annual return by over a percentage point. And a call in 3 years is not a remote risk: with the bond priced well above par, yields are already below the 8.50% coupon, so refinancing is attractive for the bank.
Yield to Worst: The Number to Quote

markDefs.definition: The lowest of the yield to maturity and the yields to every possible call date. The minimum return you can expect if the issuer pays in full and acts in its own interest.

children.text: Many callable bonds have several call dates, sometimes with call prices that step down towards par. The rule is simple: calculate the yield to every call date and to maturity, and take the lowest. That is the
yield to worst
, and it is the only honest yield for comparing a callable bond with anything else.

body.caption: Illustrative 9.20% annual-coupon NCD, 8 years to maturity, priced at ₹106.00 on a coupon date

body.text: Notice that the worst case here is the first call, even though its call price of ₹102 is the highest. A ₹2 call premium does not compensate for losing ₹4 (from ₹106 down to ₹102) in just three years. Always compute every scenario; do not assume the lowest call price or the latest date is the worst.

children.text: Discount Bonds: The Call Is Not the Worst Case

Now suppose yields rise and the same 8.50% Tier 2 bond falls to ₹96. A call at ₹100 in three years would now be good news: you would gain ₹4 in three years instead of ten. Its yield to call is 10.11%, above the 9.13% yield to maturity. But the bank has no reason to call a bond paying 8.50% when fresh money costs more than that. So for a discount bond, the yield to worst is usually the yield to maturity.

columns.label: Callable bond at a premium
points: Coupon is above market yields, so calling is attractive for the issuer
Yield to call is below yield to maturity
Yield to worst is usually a yield to call
Price is capped: the bond struggles to rise much above the call price

columns.label: Callable bond at a discount
points: Coupon is below market yields, so the issuer has no reason to call
Yield to call is above yield to maturity
Yield to worst is the yield to maturity
Behaves much like an ordinary, non-callable bond

body.title: Which yield should you use?
body.question: An illustrative NCD with an 8.75% annual coupon and 6 years to maturity is callable at par in 2 years. It trades at ₹97.20. Its yield to maturity is 9.38% and its yield to call is 10.37%. Which yield should you use to compare it with other bonds?
options: 10.37%, because the call date comes first
9.38%, because at a discount the issuer is unlikely to call, and it is the lower of the two
Neither, because callable bonds cannot be compared with other bonds
body.explanation: Yield to worst is the lower of the two: 9.38%. The bond trades below par, meaning its 8.75% coupon is below current market yields, so the issuer gains nothing by calling it early. Assuming the 10.37% call scenario would overstate your likely return.

body.title: Calculate a yield to call
body.prompt: An illustrative bank bond pays a 9% annual coupon and is callable at par in exactly one year. It trades at ₹102 per ₹100 face value, just after a coupon payment. If it is called in one year, what is your yield to call? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: With one year to the call, you pay ₹102 and receive ₹9 coupon plus ₹100 call price, ₹109 in total. YTC = ₹109 ÷ ₹102 − 1 = 6.86%. If the bond had 5 years to maturity, its YTM at ₹102 would be about 8.49%, so the call would cost you more than 1.6 percentage points a year.

children.text: The Price Ceiling on Callable Bonds

The call option does not just lower your yield. It also caps your upside. When yields fall, an ordinary 10-year bond's price rises sharply. A callable bond's price cannot rise far above its call price, because buyers know it will likely be redeemed at that price soon. The chart compares the 8.50% Tier 2 bond priced to maturity (as if it were not callable) with its price on a yield-to-worst basis, a common first-cut convention on bond desks.

body.title: 8.50% Bond: Non-Callable Price vs Yield-to-Worst Price with a 3-Year Call at ₹100

body.label: Upside lost to the call when yields fall to 6%
body.context: ₹118.40 non-callable vs ₹106.68 priced to the call. On the way down, when yields rise, the two lines are identical: you keep all the downside.

children.text: That lopsided shape, limited gains when yields fall but full losses when they rise, is called negative convexity. Chapter 4 measures it properly. Real market prices for callable bonds usually sit slightly below the yield-to-worst line, because buyers also charge for the uncertainty of not knowing whether the call will be exercised.

body.text: AT1 bonds carry risks that no yield calculation captures. There is no maturity date, the bank can skip coupons, and under RBI rules the bonds can be written down if the bank's capital falls below a trigger or it is deemed non-viable. Yes Bank's AT1 bondholders saw their bonds written off in March 2020 as part of its reconstruction. In March 2021, SEBI also directed mutual funds to value perpetual bonds as though they mature 100 years from issue rather than at the first call date, phased in over two years, precisely because calls are not guaranteed. Never treat the yield to call on an AT1 bond as a promised return.

body.title: Name the conservative yield
body.textWithBlank: For a bond with several call dates, the lowest of its yield to maturity and all its yields to call is the yield to ___.
body.explanation: Yield to worst assumes the issuer redeems on whichever date is least favourable to you, which is exactly what a rational issuer does.

markDefs.definition: A bond that gives the investor the right to sell it back to the issuer at a set price on set dates before maturity.

children.text: A
puttable bond

is the mirror image of a callable one: the option belongs to you. You will exercise it if rates rise, so you can reinvest at the higher rates, or if the issuer's credit weakens and you want your money back. Yield to put is calculated exactly like yield to call, using the put date and put price. Because the option works in your favour, a puttable bond trades at a higher price, and a lower yield, than an otherwise identical plain bond. Some Indian PSU and corporate NCDs have come with both call and put options on the same date.

body.title: Vivek's "8% for seven years"
body.scenario: Vivek Malhotra, a 52-year-old chartered accountant in Mumbai, is offered ₹50 lakh face value of an illustrative private bank Tier 2 bond through his wealth manager. Terms: 8.75% annual coupon, 7 years to maturity, callable at par in 2 years (subject to RBI approval). It trades on a coupon date at ₹103.80, so the purchase costs ₹51.90 lakh. The wealth manager's note says: "YTM 8.02%. Lock in 8% for seven years." Vivek plans to use the bond to fund his retirement income from age 59.
body.prompt: Calculate the yield to call, identify the yield to worst, explain what happens to Vivek's plan if the bond is called, and list what he should check before buying.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Yield to maturity at ₹103.80 over 7 years: 8.02%, as the note says.
2. Yield to call: pay ₹103.80, receive ₹8.75 at the end of year 1, and ₹8.75 plus ₹100 at the end of year 2. Solving gives about 6.66%.
3. Yield to worst is 6.66%. The bond is at a premium, so its 8.75% coupon is above current yields, which is exactly when a bank is most likely to call.
4. If called in 2 years: Vivek receives ₹4.375 lakh of coupons each year and ₹50 lakh back, against ₹51.90 lakh paid. His "seven-year 8% lock-in" becomes a two-year investment at about 6.66%, and he must reinvest ₹50 lakh at whatever lower rates caused the call.
5. The upside is capped too: if yields fall further, the price will struggle to rise much above ₹100 because the call is near.
6. Before buying, Vivek should: (a) ask for the yield to worst in writing, not just the YTM; (b) read the information memorandum for every call date, call price and the RBI approval condition; (c) check the bank's capital adequacy and the latest rating rationale, since Tier 2 bonds rank below depositors; (d) check recent secondary trades on the NSE or BSE RFQ platforms for liquidity; and (e) compare 6.66% with a non-callable AAA PSU bond or a G-Sec of 2 to 7 years, which may offer similar yield without the call risk.

body.title: Before buying any callable bond
steps: Find every call date and call price in the offer document or information memorandum.
Calculate the yield to each call date and to maturity, using the current price.
Take the lowest as the yield to worst, and compare bonds only on that number.
If the bond trades at a premium, assume it will be called on the first attractive date.
Plan for reinvesting the full principal at the call date, possibly at lower rates.
For AT1 bonds, remember there is no maturity, coupons can be skipped and principal can be written down.
Check liquidity on the NSE or BSE RFQ platforms; many callable bonds trade rarely.

cards.definition: A bond the issuer can redeem before maturity on set dates at a set price.
The price the issuer pays to redeem early. Often face value, sometimes with a small premium.
Annualised return if bought at today's price and redeemed on a call date at the call price.
The lowest of the YTM and all YTCs. The yield to compare callable bonds on.
A bond the investor can sell back to the issuer early. The option works in the investor's favour.
Price gains capped when yields fall, full losses when yields rise. Typical of callable bonds near their call price.

points: A call option lets the issuer repay early, and it will do so when rates have fallen below the coupon, which is bad timing for you.
Yield to call uses the YTM equation with the call date as the end date and the call price as the final payment.
Yield to worst is the lowest of the YTM and every YTC. Compare callable bonds only on YTW.
For premium bonds, YTW is usually a yield to call: the 8.50% Tier 2 bond at ₹104.50 yields 7.83% to maturity but 6.79% to worst.
For discount bonds, the issuer has no reason to call, so YTW is usually the YTM.
Callable bonds cap your gains when yields fall but give you full losses when yields rise: negative convexity.
AT1 bonds add coupon-skip and write-down risk that no yield measure captures, as Yes Bank AT1 holders learned in 2020.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Bonds, prices, call terms and investors are illustrative unless named. Bank Tier 2 and AT1 bonds are complex, carry risks beyond interest rates, and calls are subject to RBI approval and issuer discretion. Read the information memorandum and latest rating rationale, and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
